title: Scale of the Universe & Patterns in the Sky
intro: Where we sit in the universe and how big and old it is, how Earth moves through space, and how the sky looks from Earth: constellations, the celestial sphere, angles and latitude. For every number, learn what it means and why it matters.

sections.title: Our cosmic address
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: page 1 (figure from textbook Figure 1.1)

img.alt: A set of framed pictures, each inside the next bigger one: Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way Galaxy, the Local Group, the Local Supercluster, all set in the cosmic web of the universe.

steps.title: From Earth to the universe
bullets: Our address, small to big: Earth, **Solar System**, Milky Way Galaxy, Local Group, **Local Supercluster** (Laniakea), Universe.
The Solar System is the Sun plus planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The Sun is just one ordinary star.
The Milky Way is a disk-shaped group of 100+ billion stars held together by gravity. We live a little over halfway from its centre to the edge of the disk.

steps.title: Bigger groupings of galaxies
bullets: The **Local Group** has 80+ galaxies, mostly small ones. The Milky Way and Andromeda are the two largest.
The Local Group sits on the outskirts of the **Local Supercluster**. Laniakea is Hawaiian for "immense heaven".
The **universe** is the sum of all matter and energy: every supercluster, every void, everything.

steps.title: Group, cluster, supercluster
bullets: A **galaxy** is a great island of stars (millions to over a trillion) held together by gravity and orbiting a common centre.
Small collections of galaxies (up to a few dozen) are **groups**. Larger ones are clusters. A **supercluster** is a cluster of clusters.
A galaxy is about 100 million times wider than a solar system, so never mix the two up.

boxes.text: Why does each level exist? Gravity pulls things together. It holds planets around a star, stars into a galaxy, and galaxies into groups and clusters. Each level is a bigger family bound by gravity.
The names grow with the number of galaxies: a group has up to a few dozen, a cluster has more, and a supercluster is a cluster of clusters.

The textbook text and the slide both say the Local Group has more than 80 galaxies, but the textbook's chapter summary says more than 50. Use 80+. Also M31 is another name for the Andromeda Galaxy (practice question: Local Group = galaxy group with the Milky Way and M31), and the practice question defines the Solar System as everything gravitationally bound to the Sun.

sections.title: Measuring cosmic distances

steps.title: Two distance units
bullets: An **astronomical unit (AU)** is Earth's average distance from the Sun, about 150 million km (93 million miles). We use it inside the Solar System.
A **light-year (ly)** is the distance light travels in 1 year: about 10 trillion km (9.46 trillion km precisely). We use it for stars and galaxies.
A light-year measures distance, not time. "It will take me light-years to finish" makes no sense.

steps.title: Light is fast, but not instant
bullets: Light travels at **300,000 km per second**, about 8 laps around Earth every second.
Moon to Earth takes about 1 second and Sun to Earth about 8 minutes.
Sirius is about 8 ly away, the Orion Nebula about 1,350 ly, the Andromeda Galaxy about 2.5 million ly, and the farthest JWST galaxies 13+ billion ly.

steps.title: Working out a light-year
bullets: Distance = speed x time. Light moves at 300,000 km/s, and 1 year is 365 x 24 x 60 x 60 = 31,536,000 seconds.
So 1 light-year = 300,000 km/s x 31,536,000 s = about **9.46 trillion km**, which is why 10 trillion km is a good round number.
Always convert the year to seconds first, so the units match the speed in km per second.

boxes.text: Why use light-years? Kilometres get silly at star distances. The nearest star system, Alpha Centauri, is 4.4 ly away, which is about 44 trillion km. Saying 4.4 ly is far easier.
Light-YEAR sounds like time but it is a length, like a mile. It answers: how far does light get in one year?

The slide says 'about 10 trillion km (9.46 trillion km precisely)', and the textbook says the same. Use 10 trillion for quick estimates and 9.46 trillion when exact. The slide says Sirius is '~8 years away' but it means about 8 light-years (textbook: 8 light-years).

sections.title: Looking back in time
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: page 2 (figures from textbook Figures 1.3 and 1.4)

img.alt: A photo of the Andromeda Galaxy as a bright tilted disk of stars, with a small inset map showing its place in the constellation Andromeda.

steps.title: Farther away means older light
bullets: Light takes time to travel, so the farther we look, the further **back in time** we see.
A galaxy 7 billion ly away is seen as it was 7 billion years ago, when the universe was about half its present age.
Even one galaxy shows different times: Andromeda is about 100,000 ly wide, so light from its far side left about 100,000 years before light from its near side.

img.alt: A diagram of an observer with arrows to galaxies 7 billion, 12 billion and 14 billion light-years away, the last one at the edge of the observable universe.

steps.title: The observable universe
bullets: The **observable universe** is the part we can possibly see, limited by the age of the universe (about 14 billion years).
We cannot see anything more than about 14 billion ly away, because its light has not had time to reach us yet.
This is a limit on what we can see, not on the real size of the universe, which is presumed to be much larger.

boxes.text: Why do we look back in time? We see an object only when its light reaches our eyes. If the light travelled for 7 billion years, we are seeing the object as it was when the light left. Starlight is old news.
Think of a letter in the mail. A letter from a faraway place takes longer to arrive, so it tells you older news.

Do not say the observable universe is the whole universe. Slide: it is a limit on what we can observe, not the actual size. Practice question: of two galaxies at 500 million ly and 10 billion ly, the farther one looks younger (we see it as it was long ago), not older.

sections.title: Shrinking space to walking size
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: pages 2-3 (figures from textbook Figures 1.6, 1.8, 1.9, 1.10)

img.alt: The Sun's huge disk beside the planets drawn to the same scale: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto and Eris are tiny next to it.

steps.title: The Voyage model of the Solar System
bullets: Shrink everything by **1 to 10 billion**. The Sun (radius 695,000 km) becomes about 14 cm wide, a grapefruit. Jupiter becomes a marble and Earth the tip of a ballpoint pen.
Earth orbits about 15 m from the grapefruit Sun. The Moon is only about 4 cm from Earth, so all human space travel fits in the palm of your hand.
Most of the Solar System is empty. Laying out all the planetary orbits would need more than 300 football fields.

img.alt: A map of the United States on the model scale with the Sun near the east coast and Alpha Centauri on the west coast, plus a small photo of the stars Centaurus and the Southern Cross.

steps.title: Walking to the nearest star
bullets: On this scale the Sun to Pluto is only about a 600 m walk.
The Sun to Alpha Centauri (4.4 ly away) is about 4,400 km, like walking across the continental United States.
Why 4,400 km? One light-year is 10 trillion km, which becomes 1,000 km after dividing by 10 billion.

img.alt: A painting of the whole Milky Way spiral lying over a football field, with the words 'You are here' near the Sun's position.

steps.title: Scaling the Milky Way
bullets: Shrink by another factor of 1 billion (1 to 10^19). Dividing the galaxy's size (10^5 ly x 10^13 km per ly x 10^3 m per km) by a 100 m football field gives exactly 10^19.
Then **1 light-year is about 1 mm**, and the 100,000 ly Milky Way is about 100 m. Our whole Solar System is a microscopic dot near the 20-yard line, and Alpha Centauri is only 4.4 mm away.
Counting 100+ billion stars at one per second, with no breaks, would take 3,000+ years.

img.alt: A small child scooping dry sand on a beach, showing that the number of stars in the observable universe is like the number of sand grains on all beaches.

steps.title: Counting the universe
bullets: The observable universe has 100+ billion large galaxies, plus many smaller ones.
100 billion galaxies times 100 billion stars each gives about **10^22 stars**.
That is an **order of magnitude estimate** (right to about the nearest power of 10), comparable to the grains of dry sand on all Earth's beaches.

boxes.text: Why shrink things? Numbers like 150 million km do not mean much to us. A grapefruit and a pen tip 15 m apart, with the next grapefruit 4,400 km away, lets you feel how empty space is.
Sun = grapefruit, Jupiter = marble, Earth = pen tip. And on the first scale, 1 ly = 1,000 km.

Two different scales appear on the slides: 1 to 10 billion (Solar System, Alpha Centauri at 4,400 km) and 1 to 10^19 (Milky Way, 1 ly = 1 mm). Do not mix them. The textbook says the walk to the next star is about the distance to California; the slide says across the continental US. Both mean roughly 4,400 km.

sourceNotes: Mathematical Insight 1.2: Sun radius 695,000 km / 10^10 = 6.95 cm (diameter about 14 cm); scale for the galaxy to fit a 100 m field = 10^19.

sections.title: Big Bang, star life and star stuff
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: pages 3-4 (figures from textbook Figure 1.11)

img.alt: Three nested glowing cubes of different sizes full of stars, showing one region of the universe growing larger as it expands.

steps.title: The universe is expanding
bullets: Distant galaxies are moving apart, so the universe is **expanding**. Working backward gives a start, the **Big Bang**, about 14 billion years ago.
The universe as a whole expands, but gravity pulls matter together on smaller scales. Galaxies, stars and planets do not expand.
Most galaxies, including the Milky Way, formed within a few billion years after the Big Bang.

img.alt: A circle of three pictures with arrows: a star forming in a gas cloud, a shining star making elements by fusion, and a star exploding and scattering elements.

steps.title: Stars recycle matter
bullets: Gravity collapses clouds of gas and dust into stars and planets.
A star "lives" by **nuclear fusion** (light nuclei fusing into heavier ones and releasing energy) and "dies" when its fuel runs out.
Dying stars blast material back into space (the most massive ones as supernovae). It mixes into the gas between stars and forms new stars and planets, so galaxies are cosmic recycling plants.

img.alt: Earth seen from space with a person looking through a telescope, and a caption saying about 2% of the original hydrogen and helium had become heavier elements.

steps.title: We are star stuff
bullets: The early universe held only hydrogen and helium (plus a trace of lithium).
Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, iron and the rest were made inside stars, during their lives and especially in the explosions that end them.

By the time the Solar System formed (about 4.5 billion years ago), about **2%** of the galaxy's hydrogen and helium had become heavier elements. That was enough for rocky planets and the ingredients of life, hence Carl Sagan's "star stuff".

boxes.text: Why are we star stuff? Heavy elements only form in the hot, dense hearts of stars and in star explosions. Each generation of stars returned them to space, so the cloud that made our Solar System was already seeded with them.
Stars are element kitchens: fusion cooks small atoms into bigger ones, and a supernova serves the meal back into space.

The Big Bang made essentially only hydrogen and helium (trace lithium on the slide). Do not say it made carbon or iron. Also the practice question's correct life-cycle answer says gas clouds collapse under GRAVITY (not fusion) and elements are released when the star dies, 'possibly via a supernova'.

sections.title: The cosmic calendar
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: page 4 (figure from textbook Figure 1.12)

img.alt: A year calendar with the Big Bang marked on January 1, the Milky Way forming in February, Earth forming on September 3 and early life on September 22.

steps.title: 14 billion years in one year
bullets: Squeeze the 14-billion-year history of the universe into **one year**. Each month is a little more than 1 billion years.
Big Bang on Jan 1, Milky Way forms in February, Earth forms on Sept 3, and early life appears on Sept 22.
On this scale 1 day is about 38 million years and 1 second is about 440 years.

img.alt: A zoomed calendar of December with the Cambrian explosion on the 17th, the rise of the dinosaurs on the 26th and their extinction on the 30th.

steps.title: December: animals arrive
bullets: The Cambrian explosion happens on Dec 17, and the dinosaurs rise on Dec 26.
The dinosaurs die out on Dec 30. In real time that was about 66 million years ago, or only about 1.7 days before the end of the cosmic year.

img.alt: A calendar page for December 31 with early hominids at 9 PM and modern humans at 11:58 PM, and a clock face showing farming, the pyramids and Kepler and Galileo in the last seconds.

steps.title: Humans arrive at the very end
bullets: Early hominids appear at 9:00 PM on Dec 31 and modern humans at 11:58 PM.
Agriculture starts about 25 seconds before midnight, the pyramids about 11 seconds, and Kepler and Galileo about 1 second before.
All of human civilization fits into the last half-minute of the cosmic year.

boxes.text: Why compress time? A billion years is too long to imagine. On a one-year calendar, 1 second stands for about 440 years (14 billion years divided by about 31.5 million seconds in a year), so a human lifetime is a blink.
Picture New Year's Eve: the Earth party starts in September, but people only turn up in the last two minutes.

Earth forms on Sept 3, not at the start: the Milky Way (February) and many generations of stars come first. The 440 years per second figure is derived (outside source) from 14 billion / 31.5 million. The textbook says dinosaurs died about 66 million years ago; the slide only gives the calendar date Dec 30.

sections.title: Spaceship Earth: motions you cannot feel
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: pages 4-6; ASTR207 TopHat sep8.pdf: page 1 (figures from textbook Figures 1.13-1.16, 1.18)

img.alt: A stack of pictures showing Earth's motions from the smallest to the largest: spinning, orbiting the Sun, moving among nearby stars, orbiting the Milky Way, moving toward Andromeda and the expanding universe.

steps.title: A table of our motions
bullets: Rotation: more than 1,000 km/h near the equator, once per day. Orbit around the Sun: about **107,000 km/h**, once per year.
Motion among nearby stars: about 70,000 km/h in an essentially random direction. Orbit around the Milky Way's centre: about **800,000 km/h**, once per 230 million years.
The Milky Way and Andromeda approach each other at about 300,000 km/h. More distant galaxies recede faster, some near the speed of light.

img.alt: Earth orbiting the Sun on a flat ecliptic plane, with its axis tilted 23.5 degrees and always pointing toward Polaris.

steps.title: Spin, tilt and orbit
bullets: Earth rotates west to east (counterclockwise seen from above the North Pole), so the Sun and stars seem to rise in the east and set in the west.
Earth's orbit defines the **ecliptic plane**. Its axis is tilted 23.5 degrees from a line perpendicular to that plane and points toward **Polaris**.
Earth orbits in the same direction it spins because it formed in a spinning disk of gas around the young Sun. That is not a coincidence.

img.alt: A globe with arrows showing how fast the ground moves as Earth spins: 0 km/h at the pole, 1,100 km/h in the middle latitudes and 1,670 km/h at the equator.

steps.title: How fast does Earth spin and orbit?
bullets: Spin speed depends on where you stand: 0 km/h at the pole, about 1,100 km/h in the middle latitudes and about 1,670 km/h at the equator. At the equator it is 2 x pi x 6,378 km / 24 h.
Orbit speed: 2 x pi x 150 million km, divided by 1 year (8,760 h), is about 107,000 km/h.
Most speeding bullets travel between 500 and 1,000 km/h, so Earth's orbital speed is more than 100 times that.

img.alt: A painting of the Milky Way with a cube of randomly moving nearby stars at 70,000 km/h and a ring showing the Sun's 230-million-year orbit, 27,000 light-years from the center.

steps.title: Motion inside the Milky Way
bullets: Nearby stars drift randomly at about 70,000 km/h, but they are so far away that constellations only change noticeably after 10,000+ years.
Our Solar System is about 27,000 ly from the galactic centre and goes around once every 230 million years.
Four and a half billion years divided by about 225 to 230 million years gives roughly **20 laps** around the galaxy so far.

img.alt: An edge-on painting of the Milky Way as a thin bright disk, with notes that most light comes from the disk but most of the mass lies unseen in a halo around it.

steps.title: Orbit speeds reveal dark matter
bullets: Stars' orbital speeds show that most of the galaxy's mass is invisible and sits in a halo around the visible disk.
This unseen mass is called **dark matter**.
Stars far from the centre move much faster than the visible matter alone can explain, so something extra must be pulling on them with gravity.

boxes.text: Why do we feel none of this? We move smoothly at nearly constant speed together with the ground, the air and everything around us, so nothing pushes on us. Why do all planets orbit the same way? They formed from one spinning disk of gas.
Slowest to fastest: spin (about 1,000), wander among stars (70,000), orbit the Sun (107,000), orbit the galaxy (800,000). Even the slowest of the last three beats a rifle bullet (about 3,000 km/h).

The in-class questions use different numbers from the slide: Sun's speed among stars ~80,000+ or ~10,000 km/h and Earth's orbit ~108,000 or ~80,000 km/h, and Earth's rotation 1,670 km/h. The slide and textbook give 70,000 and ~107,000, and rotation 'more than 1,000'. Use the slide values, and note the ORDER slowest to fastest is the same. The slide says 230 million years per galactic orbit; the in-class question uses 225 million (both give about 20 laps). Practice question: 'the Sun orbits the centre of the local stellar neighbourhood' is NOT an observed motion (nearby stars move randomly).

sections.title: Hubble, raisin cakes and dark energy
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: pages 6-7; ASTR207 TopHat sep8.pdf: pages 1-2 (figures from textbook Figure 1.17 and the Top Hat page)

steps.title: Hubble's two discoveries
bullets: Inside the Local Group, galaxies move fairly randomly. The Milky Way and Andromeda are approaching each other at about 300,000 km/h, but any collision is billions of years away.
Outside the Local Group, Edwin Hubble found that virtually **every galaxy is moving away** from us, and **more distant galaxies move away faster**.
This is explained by the **expansion of the universe itself**, not by our galaxy being special or central.

img.alt: Coins on a rubber sheet that gets farther apart as the sheet is stretched, though the coins do not move across it.

steps.title: Coins on a stretching sheet
bullets: When a rubber sheet stretches, the coins on it get farther apart even though they do not move across the sheet.
This is a good example of uniform expansion: the sheet between the coins grows.
Galaxies behave like the coins: the space between them stretches.

img.alt: A raisin cake before baking with raisins 1 cm apart, and after baking with raisins 3 cm apart, with the Local Raisin marked and three neighbors numbered 1, 2 and 3.

steps.title: The raisin cake analogy
bullets: Raisins sit 1 cm apart in a cake that expands as it bakes. From any one raisin (the "Local Raisin"), all other raisins move away, and farther ones move away faster.
The cake between them is what grows, so no raisin is more "central" than any other. The same is true for galaxies.
In the picture every distance triples in 1 hour (1 cm becomes 3 cm). The next step shows what each raisin sees.

img.alt: A table of raisin number, starting distance, distance after baking and speed: raisin 1 is 1 cm, 3 cm, 2 cm per hour; raisin 2 is 2 cm, 6 cm, 4 cm per hour; raisin 3 is 3 cm, 9 cm, 6 cm per hour.

steps.title: Reading the raisin table
bullets: Raisin 1 goes from 1 cm to 3 cm in 1 hour, so it moves away at 2 cm/h. Raisin 2 goes from 2 cm to 6 cm, which is 4 cm/h. Raisin 3 goes from 3 cm to 9 cm, which is 6 cm/h.
Double the starting distance and you double the speed, so speed is proportional to distance. This is the same pattern Hubble found for galaxies.
A raisin that starts 10 cm away would end 30 cm away and move at 20 cm/h.

steps.title: Age, gravity and dark energy
bullets: The expansion rate lets astronomers work out the age of the universe, about 14 billion years. A faster past expansion would mean a younger universe.
We are not expanding: gravity overcomes expansion on small scales. Only the space between distant, unbound galaxies grows.
**Dark energy** is a different mystery. It was discovered because the expansion is accelerating, and it makes up the majority of the universe's total energy.

boxes.text: Why do farther galaxies move away faster? There is more stretching space between us and them. Double the distance and you double the amount of space that grows, so you double the speed. That is why the graph of speed against distance is a straight line with a positive slope.
Rubber sheet or raisin cake: wherever you stand, everyone else seems to run away from you, and the farthest run fastest. There is no centre.

Do not confuse dark matter (unseen mass, from galaxy rotation) with dark energy (accelerating expansion, most of the energy). Also, 'more distant galaxies move away faster' is for galaxies OUTSIDE the Local Group. The in-class answer says raisin 1 does not travel at raisin 3's speed: speed depends on starting distance. The numbers in the cake-tripling example come from the textbook, not the slide.

sections.title: Constellations and the celestial sphere
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: pages 8-9 and ASTR207 LEC SEP08 (1).pdf: pages 1-2 (figures from textbook Figures 2.2-2.5)

img.alt: Orion and its neighbors with straight outlines marking the official constellation borders and yellow lines joining the familiar star patterns, as seen by a person looking south on a winter evening.

steps.title: A constellation is a patch of sky
bullets: On a clear, dark, moonless night you can see 2,000+ stars with the naked eye, plus the Milky Way band.

A **constellation** is a region of sky with official borders, not just the star pattern. In the picture the straight outlines are borders and the yellow lines are only the familiar patterns. Every point in the sky is in some constellation, like every point on a map is in some state.

There are **88** official constellations, with borders set in **1928** by the International Astronomical Union (IAU). Northern names come from the ancient Middle East, southern names from 17th-century European explorers.

img.alt: A globe with constellations painted on it surrounding Earth, with arrows showing that the stars really lie at very different distances.

bullets: Stars in one constellation look close together but may be at very different distances. We lack depth perception when we look into space.
The ancient Greeks took this for reality and pictured stars fixed on a giant sphere around Earth. It is still a handy model for mapping the sky.

img.alt: A sphere around Earth with the north and south celestial poles above Earth's poles, the celestial equator around the middle, and the tilted ecliptic circle crossing it at 23.5 degrees.

steps.title: Poles, equator and ecliptic
bullets: Key marks: the north and south **celestial poles** (directly above Earth's poles), the celestial equator (Earth's equator projected into space), and the **ecliptic** (the Sun's apparent yearly path, crossing the celestial equator at 23.5 degrees).

img.alt: A painting of our galaxy as a flat spiral with the Solar System marked, showing that looking along the galactic plane sees many stars while looking out of it gives a clear view of the distant universe.

steps.title: The Milky Way in our sky
bullets: The band of light called the Milky Way circles the whole celestial sphere through a dozen constellations. It is most vivid from the Southern Hemisphere.
The band is a side-on view of our galaxy's disk (the **galactic plane**) from inside it. Looking along the disk shows many stars. Looking away from it gives a clear view of the distant universe.
The band is wider toward Sagittarius (the galactic centre and bulge). Dust lanes block our view beyond a few thousand ly, so radio, infrared and X-ray telescopes were needed to see more.

boxes.text: Why does the sky look like a sphere? We have no sense of depth for faraway lights, so every star seems the same distance away, painted on the inside of a ball. Why is the ecliptic tilted 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator? Because Earth's axis is tilted by 23.5 degrees.
The celestial equator is Earth's equator thrown up onto the sky. The ecliptic is the Sun's yearly road across the stars.

A constellation is a region with borders, not only the stick figure. The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent path over a YEAR, not its daily path across the sky (practice question Q12, false option). The textbook says 12 traditional zodiac constellations lie along the ecliptic but the official borders include a 13th, Ophiuchus (practice option A). The 'Milky Way' band and the Milky Way galaxy are two views of the same thing. Practice Q13 (galactic plane at 63 degrees to the celestial equator) uses a number found in neither slides nor textbook.

steps.title: Your sky is a dome
bullets: From anywhere on Earth the sky looks like a dome. You see only half the celestial sphere because the ground blocks the rest.
The horizon has altitude 0 degrees and the **zenith** (straight overhead) has altitude 90 degrees. The meridian is an imaginary half-circle from due south through the zenith to due north.

Any object is located by its direction (azimuth, degrees clockwise from due north) and its **altitude** (degrees above the horizon). The star in the picture is at altitude 60 degrees toward the southeast.

img.alt: Two night-sky scenes: the Moon spanning half a degree, and the Big Dipper's pointer stars 5 degrees apart with the Southern Cross 6 degrees long.

bullets: With no depth perception, we can only say how big or how far apart things look, not how big or far they are.
**Angular size** is the angle an object seems to span. The Sun and Moon both span about 0.5 degrees, even though the Sun is about 400 times bigger and about 400 times farther away.
**Angular distance** is the angle between two objects: about 5 degrees between the Big Dipper's pointer stars and about 6 degrees for the length of the Southern Cross.

img.alt: A person stretching an arm out to the sky, with one hand spread to show about 20 degrees, a fist showing about 10 degrees and a finger width showing 1 degree.

steps.title: Measuring angles with your hand
bullets: At arm's length your hand works as a ruler: a fist is about **10 degrees** across, a spread hand about 20 degrees and a little finger about 1 degree.
These are angles, not lengths, so they work for any object in the sky.

img.alt: A circle with a 1 degree slice opened up into 60 arcminutes, and one arcminute opened up into 60 arcseconds.

steps.title: Degrees, arcminutes, arcseconds
bullets: 1 degree = 60 **arcminutes** and 1 arcminute = 60 **arcseconds**, so 1 degree = 3,600 arcseconds.
Distance from the zenith = 90 degrees minus altitude. A star at altitude 80 degrees is 10 degrees, or 600 arcminutes, from the zenith.

img.slide: textbook PDF p.50 / Mathematical Insight 2.1 Figure 1
img.alt: Two diagrams: an eye looking at an object that looks smaller as it moves farther away, and a circle around the eye showing that a small object is like a small piece of the circle.

steps.title: The small-angle formula
bullets: **angular size = physical size x 360 degrees / (2 x pi x distance)**. Give any two and you can find the third.
Example: the Moon spans about 0.5 degrees at a distance of 380,000 km, so its diameter is 0.5 x 2 x pi x 380,000 / 360 = about 3,300 km.
Doubling the distance halves the angular size. A 1 m ball seen from 115 m away spans about 0.5 degrees, the same as the Moon.

boxes.text: Why do the Sun and Moon look equally big? The formula shows the angle depends on size divided by distance. The Sun is about 400 times bigger but about 400 times farther, so the ratio, and the angle, is almost the same.
Arcminutes work like clock minutes: 60 to the hour, and 60 arcminutes to the degree. Arcseconds are the next step down, 60 to the arcminute.

A star at altitude 80 degrees is 10 degrees (600 arcminutes) from the zenith, not 80 degrees or 10 arcminutes (practice Q11: answer 600). Altitude is measured from the horizon; zenith distance from straight up. Azimuth is clockwise from due NORTH. Slide: Sun and Moon ~0.5 degrees; the textbook writes 1/2 degree.

sections.title: Rising, setting and your latitude
sections.slides: ASTR207 LEC SEP08.pdf: pages 9-10; ASTR207 LEC SEP08 (1).pdf: pages 2-3 (figures from textbook Figures 2.9-2.14)

img.alt: The celestial sphere around Earth with red arrows showing it seeming to turn once a day around the line joining the celestial poles.

steps.title: Why stars rise and set
bullets: The sky seems to turn around us every day. Really **Earth rotates** west to east, not the universe.
We model this as the celestial sphere spinning around Earth.
That is why stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

img.alt: The local sky at latitude 40 degrees north: a tilted horizon plane cutting the celestial sphere, with one circumpolar circle entirely above it, one star never seen, and others rising and setting.

steps.title: Circumpolar stars
bullets: Seen from latitude 40 degrees N: stars near the north celestial pole are **circumpolar**. They never set and circle counterclockwise above the horizon.
Stars near the opposite (south) celestial pole never rise at all. All other stars rise in the east and set in the west.
In the Southern Hemisphere the same logic holds around the south celestial pole, but the circles run clockwise.

img.alt: A globe with lines of latitude and longitude, the equator and the prime meridian through Greenwich, and Miami marked at 26 degrees north and 80 degrees west.

steps.title: Latitude and longitude
bullets: **Latitude** is north-south position (0 degrees at the equator, 90 degrees N or S at the poles). **Longitude** is east-west, 0 degrees at Greenwich.
The sky depends on latitude only, not longitude. Charleston, SC and San Diego, CA share a latitude and see the same night sky.

img.alt: Two globes showing the local sky: at the North Pole the north celestial pole is overhead at 90 degrees, and at latitude 34 degrees south the south celestial pole is 34 degrees above the horizon.

steps.title: Pole height equals latitude
bullets: Key fact: **the altitude of the visible celestial pole equals your latitude**. At latitude 34 degrees S, the south celestial pole is 34 degrees above the south horizon.
At the North Pole (90 degrees N) the north celestial pole is straight overhead. At the equator it sits on the horizon, at 0 degrees.

img.alt: Looking north in the Northern Hemisphere: the Big Dipper's pointer stars point to Polaris and the Big Dipper and Little Dipper circle counterclockwise around it over 6 hours.

steps.title: Finding the north celestial pole
bullets: Polaris lies within 1 degree of the north celestial pole, so the whole sky turns counterclockwise around it. The pointer stars of the Big Dipper lead to Polaris.
Polaris is special only because it sits near the pole. It is not the brightest star.

img.alt: Looking south in the Southern Hemisphere: the Southern Cross points to the south celestial pole about 4 cross lengths away, and turns clockwise around it over 6 hours.

steps.title: Finding the south celestial pole
bullets: No bright star marks the south celestial pole. Extend the long axis of the Southern Cross about 4 cross lengths to find it.

img.alt: A globe for the North Pole with the north celestial pole directly overhead at 90 degrees and the celestial equator along the horizon.

steps.title: The North Pole extreme
bullets: At the North Pole (90 degrees N) you can only ever see the northern half of the celestial sphere, and all of it is circumpolar.
That is why the Sun stays up for 6 continuous months there: for half the year the Sun is on the northern half of the celestial sphere.

img.alt: A top view of Earth's orbit with the Sun seen against the zodiac constellations around the ecliptic, with arrows for the day and night directions on August 21 pointing to Leo and Aquarius.

steps.title: The sky changes through the year
bullets: As Earth orbits, the Sun appears to move steadily eastward along the ecliptic, in front of different constellations.
The constellation the Sun is in is lost in the daytime sky. The one opposite the Sun is up all night.
Six months later the Sun is at the opposite end of the ecliptic, so some constellations that were hidden are now visible at night.

boxes.text: Why does the pole's altitude equal your latitude? At the North Pole the north celestial pole is straight overhead (90 degrees), the same as the latitude. At the equator it sits on the horizon (0 degrees). In between it climbs steadily as you go north.
Pole height = latitude. If the North Star is 40 degrees up, you are at 40 degrees N.

Polaris is NOT the brightest star; it is special only because it sits near the north celestial pole. Latitude, not longitude, sets your sky. At the poles every visible star is circumpolar (practice Q9, option C false). You see only about half of the stars on a given night (option E is the true one). The 'sky through the year' step is from the textbook 2.1 and practice Q10; the slides state the question but give text only up to the North Pole.

cards.front: What is our cosmic address, from Earth up to the universe?
cards.back: Earth, Solar System, Milky Way Galaxy, Local Group, Local Supercluster (Laniakea), Universe.
cards.short: Earth, Solar System, Milky Way, Group, Supercluster

cards.back: The Sun plus everything held by its gravity: planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The Sun is just one star.
cards.short: Sun plus everything it holds by gravity

cards.back: A galaxy is a great island of stars held by gravity and orbiting a common centre. The Milky Way has 100+ billion stars, and we sit a little over halfway out from its centre.
cards.short: Island of stars held by gravity

cards.back: A collection of 80+ galaxies, mostly small. The Milky Way and Andromeda are the two largest.
cards.short: 80+ galaxies; Milky Way and Andromeda largest

cards.front: Group, cluster and supercluster of galaxies
cards.back: Group: up to a few dozen galaxies. Cluster: a larger collection. Supercluster: a region where groups and clusters are packed densely, a cluster of clusters (Local Supercluster = Laniakea).
cards.short: Dozens, larger, then a cluster of clusters

cards.back: The sum total of all matter and energy, including all superclusters, voids and everything within them.
cards.short: All matter and energy together

cards.back: Earth's average distance from the Sun, about 150 million km (93 million miles). Used inside the Solar System.
cards.short: Earth-Sun distance, 150 million km

cards.back: The distance light travels in one year, about 10 trillion km (9.46 trillion km precisely). It is a distance, not a time.
cards.short: Distance light covers in a year

cards.front: Speed of light and light travel times
cards.back: 300,000 km/s. Moon to Earth about 1+ second, Sun to Earth about 8 minutes.
cards.short: 300,000 km/s; 1 second; 8 minutes

cards.back: Sirius about 8 ly, Orion Nebula about 1,350 ly, Andromeda about 2.5 million ly, most distant JWST galaxies 13+ billion ly.
cards.short: 8; 1,350; 2.5 million; 13+ billion ly

cards.back: The farther away we look, the further back in time we see, because light takes time to arrive. A galaxy 7 billion ly away is seen as it was 7 billion years ago. Andromeda's far side shows light about 100,000 years older than its near side.
cards.short: Farther away means seeing further back

cards.back: The part of the universe we can possibly see, limited by the universe's age (about 14 billion years). We cannot see beyond about 14 billion ly. It is a limit on what we observe, not the universe's actual size.
cards.short: Limited by age: about 14 billion ly

cards.back: The Solar System shrunk 1 to 10 billion. Sun = grapefruit, Jupiter = marble, Earth = ballpoint tip about 15 m from the Sun, Moon about 4 cm from Earth. Sun to Pluto is about 600 m.
cards.short: 1 to 10 billion; Sun a grapefruit

cards.front: Alpha Centauri on the Voyage scale
cards.back: The Sun to Alpha Centauri (4.4 ly) is about 4,400 km on the 1-to-10-billion scale, like walking across the continental US. One light-year is 1,000 km on this scale.
cards.short: About 4,400 km, across the continent

cards.back: 1 ly is about 1 mm, so the 100,000 ly Milky Way is about 100 m (a football field). The Solar System is a microscopic dot. Counting its 100+ billion stars at one per second takes 3,000+ years.
cards.short: 1 ly = 1 mm; galaxy = 100 m

cards.front: Number of stars in the observable universe
cards.back: About 10^22: 100 billion galaxies times 100 billion stars each. It is an order of magnitude estimate, comparable to the grains of dry sand on all Earth's beaches.
cards.short: About 10^22; order of magnitude estimate

cards.back: Distant galaxies move apart, so working backward the universe started in the Big Bang about 14 billion years ago. Gravity holds galaxies, stars and planets together, so they do not expand.
cards.short: Start about 14 billion years ago

cards.back: Gas and dust collapse under gravity into stars. Stars make energy and elements by nuclear fusion. When they die (the most massive in supernovae) they return material to space for new stars and planets.
cards.short: Collapse, fuse, die, recycle into new stars

cards.back: Early on there was only hydrogen, helium and trace lithium. Heavier elements were made inside stars. By the Solar System's birth about 2% of the galaxy's hydrogen and helium had become heavier elements: we are star stuff.
cards.short: Elements made in earlier stars; about 2%

cards.back: The 14-billion-year history squeezed into one year, each month a little over 1 billion years. All of human civilization fits into the last half-minute.
cards.short: 14 billion years in one year

cards.back: Big Bang Jan 1, Milky Way February, Earth Sept 3, early life Sept 22, Cambrian Dec 17, dinosaurs rise Dec 26 and die Dec 30, modern humans 11:58 PM Dec 31.
cards.short: Earth Sept 3; dinosaurs gone Dec 30

cards.back: Rotation >1,000 km/h (equator), orbit around the Sun about 107,000 km/h, motion among nearby stars about 70,000 km/h, orbit of the Milky Way about 800,000 km/h, approach to Andromeda about 300,000 km/h.
The Solar System is about 27,000 ly from the galactic centre and orbits once every about 230 million years. Over 4.5 billion years that is about 20 orbits.
cards.short: One lap takes about 230 million years

cards.back: Tilted 23.5 degrees from a line perpendicular to the ecliptic plane, pointing toward Polaris. Earth spins and orbits in the same direction because it formed in a spinning disk of gas.
cards.short: Tilted 23.5 degrees, points at Polaris

cards.back: Stars' orbital speeds show most of a galaxy's mass is unseen, in a halo around the disk. This unseen mass is dark matter.
cards.short: Unseen halo mass shown by orbit speeds

cards.back: A separate mystery discovered because the universe's expansion is accelerating. It makes up the majority of the universe's total energy.
cards.short: Accelerating expansion; most of the energy

cards.back: Outside the Local Group, virtually every galaxy moves away from us, and more distant galaxies move away faster. This shows the universe is expanding.
cards.short: Galaxies recede; farther ones faster

cards.back: In an expanding cake, every raisin sees all others moving away, farther ones faster, because the cake between them grows. Space itself expands between galaxies, and no galaxy is the centre.
cards.short: Space stretches; no galaxy is central

cards.back: A region of sky with official borders (every point belongs to one). There are 88, with borders set in 1928 by the IAU.
cards.short: Sky region with borders; 88 of them

cards.back: An illusion: stars seem to lie on a sphere around Earth because we lack depth perception in space. Stars in a constellation can be at very different distances. It is still useful for mapping.
cards.short: Illusion from missing depth perception

cards.back: Celestial poles lie above Earth's poles. The celestial equator is Earth's equator projected into space. The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent yearly path, crossing the celestial equator at 23.5 degrees.
cards.short: Ecliptic: Sun's yearly path, 23.5 degrees

cards.front: Milky Way band in the sky
cards.back: A side-on view of our galaxy's disk (the galactic plane) from inside it, circling the whole sky. It looks widest toward Sagittarius, the galactic centre.
cards.short: Side view of our galaxy's disk

cards.back: The local sky is a dome (half the celestial sphere). Altitude is degrees above the horizon (zenith = 90 degrees). Azimuth is degrees clockwise from due north.
cards.short: Dome sky; altitude up, azimuth around

cards.back: Angular size is the angle an object appears to span; angular distance is the angle between two objects. Sun and Moon both span about 0.5 degrees (Sun about 400 times bigger and 400 times farther).
cards.short: Apparent angle spanned; Sun equals Moon

cards.back: 1 degree = 60 arcminutes, 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds. A star 10 degrees from the zenith (altitude 80 degrees) is 600 arcminutes away.
cards.short: 60 arcminutes per degree; 60 arcseconds

cards.back: angular size = physical size x 360 degrees / (2 x pi x distance). Any two quantities give the third.
cards.short: Size times 360 over 2 pi distance

cards.back: Earth rotates west to east, so the sky seems to turn daily. Stars rise in the east and set in the west.
cards.short: Earth's spin makes stars rise and set

cards.back: From 40 degrees N, stars near the north celestial pole never set (they circle counterclockwise). Stars near the south celestial pole never rise. Southern Hemisphere circles run clockwise.
cards.short: Never set near the visible pole

cards.back: The altitude of the visible celestial pole equals your latitude. The sky depends on latitude only, not longitude. Polaris is within 1 degree of the north pole but is not the brightest star. At the North Pole all visible stars are circumpolar, so the Sun stays up for 6 months.
cards.short: Pole altitude equals latitude; not longitude

cards.back: The Sun appears to move along the ecliptic over a year. Constellations near it are lost in daylight. Six months later the Sun is at the opposite end, so different constellations show at night.
cards.short: Sun's position changes which stars appear

cards.front: How is a light-year worked out?
cards.back: Distance = speed x time. 1 ly = 300,000 km/s x (365 x 24 x 60 x 60 s) = 300,000 x 31,536,000 = about 9.46 trillion km. Always convert the year to seconds first.
cards.short: Speed of light times one year

cards.front: Spin and orbit speed of Earth by calculation
cards.back: Speed = circumference / time. Equator: 2 x pi x 6,378 km / 24 h = about 1,670 km/h. Orbit: 2 x pi x 150 million km / 8,760 h = about 107,000 km/h.
cards.short: Circumference over time gives speed

cards.front: Order of magnitude with powers of ten
cards.back: Multiply by adding exponents and divide by subtracting them. Sand grains on all beaches: (10^9 m x 10^2 m^2) / 10^-10 m^3 = 10^21, comparable to the 10^22 stars.
cards.short: Add exponents; sand grains about 10^21

cards.back: Moon: 0.5 degrees at 380,000 km gives 0.5 x 2 x pi x 380,000 / 360 = about 3,300 km wide. Headlights 1.5 m apart at 500 m: 1.5 x 360 / (2 x pi x 500) = 0.17 degrees, about 10 arcminutes.
cards.short: Moon about 3,300 km from its angle

cards.back: Distances triple in 1 hour: a raisin 1 cm away ends 3 cm away (2 cm/h), 2 cm becomes 6 cm (4 cm/h), 3 cm becomes 9 cm (6 cm/h). Speed is proportional to starting distance.
cards.short: Speed proportional to starting distance

cards.back: One year is 14 billion years, so 1 day is about 38 million years and 1 second about 440 years. The dinosaurs died about 66 million years ago, about 1.7 days before the end.
cards.short: One day is about 38 million years
cards.src: Slide 4; textbook Figure 1.12 and 1.2 (66 million years); arithmetic derived

quiz.q: What is the Solar System?
options: The Sun and the 8 major planets, including Earth.
The collection of astronomical objects that receive light and heat from the Sun.
The collection of astronomical objects that are gravitationally bound by the Sun.
The Sun and the 8 major planets, along with Pluto and various comets.
The volume of objects that extends out to 30 AU from the Sun.
quiz.why: The Solar System is the Sun plus everything it holds by gravity: planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets, not just the 8 planets.
quiz.source: Slide 1; Textbook 1.1 definitions; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q1 (practice)

quiz.q: What is the scientific distinction between a star and a planet?
options: Planets are habitable in theory, whereas stars are not.
Planets orbit stars, whereas stars do not orbit anything.
Planets are not massive enough to undergo nuclear fusion, whereas stars are.
Planets do not emit radiation, whereas stars do.
Planets are solid in composition, whereas stars are made of gas.
quiz.why: A star is massive enough that gravity makes its core hot and dense enough for sustained nuclear fusion. A planet is not. Gas giants are not solid, planets do give off some heat, and stars orbit the center of their galaxy, so the other options fail.
quiz.source: ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q2 (practice); slide 3 (stars shine by nuclear fusion); textbook 1.1

quiz.q: Using the picture of our cosmic address, what is the Local Group?
options: The group of stars closest to our Sun, which includes Proxima Centauri.
The system of bodies that includes the Sun and all objects that orbit it.
The location in the Milky Way in which our Solar System resides.
The galaxy cluster that contains the Milky Way and numerous other galaxies.
The galaxy group containing the Milky Way and Andromeda (M31).
quiz.why: The Local Group has 80+ galaxies, mostly small. The Milky Way and Andromeda (M31) are the two largest.
quiz.source: Slide 1; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q3 (practice, option rewritten)

img.alt: Framed pictures of Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way, the Local Group and the Local Supercluster, each inside a bigger frame.

quiz.q: The speed of light is 300,000 km/s. Using 1 year = 365 days, what is the length of one light-year?
quiz.why: Distance = speed x time. A year is 365 x 24 x 60 x 60 = 31,536,000 s, so 300,000 km/s x 31,536,000 s = 9.46 x 10^12 km. Skipping the 24 hours gives 3.94 x 10^11, using minutes instead of seconds gives 1.58 x 10^11, and using hours gives 2.63 x 10^9.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 1.1 (How far is a light-year?); slides 1-2

quiz.q: Look at the picture of the observable universe. Suppose two galaxies formed at about the same time. One is 500 million light-years away and the other is 10 billion light-years away. Which statement about observing them is true?
options: The first galaxy will appear older, as its light takes much longer to reach us.
The first galaxy will appear younger, as its light reaches us much more quickly.
The second galaxy will appear older, as its light reaches us much more quickly.
Since they formed at the same time, they will appear the same age.
The second galaxy will appear younger, as its light takes much longer to reach us.
quiz.why: Farther away means we see further back in time. Light from the 10-billion-ly galaxy left 10 billion years ago, when the galaxy was young.
quiz.source: Slide 2; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q5 (practice, options reordered)

img.alt: An observer with arrows to galaxies 7, 12 and 14 billion light-years away, showing that farther galaxies are seen as they were longer ago.

quiz.q: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away and about 100,000 light-years across. Which statement about the light we see from it tonight is correct?
options: Light from the near side left about 100,000 years before light from the far side.
Light from both sides left at the same moment, because we see the whole galaxy at once.
Light from the far side left about 2.5 million years before light from the near side.
Light from the far side left about 100,000 years before light from the near side.
Both sides show the galaxy exactly as it is today, because light is so fast.
quiz.why: The far side is about 100,000 light-years farther, so its light needed about 100,000 more years to arrive. To reach us at the same time, it had to leave 100,000 years earlier. We therefore see different parts of the galaxy at different times.
quiz.source: Slide 2; textbook 1.1 and Figure 1.3

quiz.q: The Sun's radius is about 695,000 km. A scale model shrinks everything by a factor of 10 billion (10^10). About how wide (diameter) is the model Sun?
options: About 1.4 cm
About 7 cm
About 14 cm
About 1.4 m
About 14 m
quiz.why: Radius: 695,000 km = 6.95 x 10^10 cm, and dividing by 10^10 gives 6.95 cm. The diameter is twice the radius, about 14 cm, the size of a large grapefruit. Quoting 7 cm forgets to double the radius.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 1.2 Example 1 and Figure 1.6; slide 2

img.alt: The Sun's disk beside the planets at the same scale, with the planets tiny by comparison.

quiz.q: A scale model must shrink the 100,000 light-year Milky Way to fit across a football field 100 m long. Use 1 ly = 10^13 km and 1 km = 10^3 m. The scale needed is 1 to
quiz.why: The galaxy is 10^5 ly x 10^13 km/ly x 10^3 m/km = 10^21 m. Divide by the field's 10^2 m: 10^21 / 10^2 = 10^19. The answer 10^21 forgets to divide by the 100 m field, and 10^10 is the scale used for the Solar System.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 1.2 Example 2; slide 3

quiz.q: Estimate the grains of dry sand on all of Earth's beaches. Total beach length is about 10^9 m, beach width x depth is about 10^2 m^2, and one grain has a volume of about 10^-10 m^3. About how many grains are there?
quiz.why: Number of grains = total volume / volume of one grain = (10^9 m x 10^2 m^2) / 10^-10 m^3 = 10^11 / 10^-10 = 10^21. Dividing by a negative exponent adds it (11 + 10 = 21). This is within a factor of 10 of the 10^22 stars in the observable universe, so the two numbers are comparable.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 1.3; slide 3

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly describes the stellar life cycle?
options: Gas clouds collapse under nuclear fusion to form stars, and the stars later expand back into gas clouds.
Gas clouds collapse under gravity to form stars, fusion makes elements that form planets, and the whole system returns to the nebula when the star explodes.
Gas clouds collapse under gravity to form stars, fusion generates light and heat, and that heat makes nearby gas clouds collapse.
Galaxies collapse under gravity to form stars, and elements are released when the star explodes.
Gas clouds collapse under gravity to form stars, fusion makes elements, and these are released into space when the star dies, possibly in a supernova.
quiz.why: Gravity forms the star, fusion builds heavier elements, and a dying star (the most massive in a supernova) returns them to space to make new stars and planets.
quiz.source: Slide 3; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q4 (practice, options shortened)

quiz.q:
Consider these statements.
I. The early universe held almost only hydrogen and helium.
II. Carbon, oxygen and iron were made inside stars.
III. By the time the Solar System formed, about 2% of the galaxy's hydrogen and helium had been turned into heavier elements.
Which are true?
options: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
all of the above
quiz.why: The Big Bang made essentially hydrogen and helium (plus a trace of lithium). Heavier elements were fused inside stars and returned to space when stars died. About 2% of the galaxy's gas had been enriched by the time our Solar System formed, enough for rocky planets and life.
quiz.source: Slides 3-4; textbook 1.2 (Star Stuff)

quiz.q: The cosmic calendar squeezes the 14-billion-year history of the universe into one 365-day year. The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. About how many days before the end of the cosmic year did this happen?
options: About 0.17 days (about 4 hours)
About 0.7 days
About 1.7 days
About 17 days
About 66 days
quiz.why: One cosmic day is 14 billion / 365 = about 38 million years. So 66 million years is 66 / 38 = about 1.7 days before midnight on Dec 31, which matches the dinosaur extinction on Dec 30.
quiz.source: Slide 4 (Dec 30); textbook 1.2 and Figure 1.12 (66 million years); arithmetic derived

quiz.q: If we plotted the speed at which galaxies move away from us against their distance, as Hubble did, what would we see?
options: An exponential curve
A quadratic curve
A line with a negative slope
An inverse relationship
A line with a positive slope
quiz.why: More distant galaxies move away proportionally faster, so the points fall on a rising straight line.
quiz.source: Slide 6; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q7 (practice, options reordered)

quiz.q: The picture shows a raisin cake in which every distance becomes 3 times larger in one hour. A raisin starts 10 cm from the Local Raisin. How fast does it move away from the Local Raisin?
options: 10 cm/h
20 cm/h
30 cm/h
40 cm/h
5 cm/h
quiz.why: It goes from 10 cm to 30 cm, so it moves 20 cm in 1 hour: 20 cm/h. Farther raisins move faster.
quiz.source: Slide 6; Textbook 1.3 raisin cake (Think about it)

img.alt: A raisin cake before baking with raisins 1 cm apart and after baking with raisins 3 cm apart, with the Local Raisin marked.

quiz.q: In the expanding raisin cake, raisin 3 starts 3 times farther from the Local Raisin than raisin 1 does. How does the speed of raisin 3 compare with raisin 1?
options: Raisin 3 moves 3 times faster.
Both move at the same speed.
Raisin 1 moves 3 times faster.
Raisin 3 moves 9 times faster.
Raisin 3 does not move.
quiz.why: In uniform expansion, speed is proportional to starting distance. Raisin 3 has more cake between it and the Local Raisin to grow.
quiz.source: Slide 6; Top Hat sep8 page 2; Textbook 1.3

quiz.q:
Consider these statements.
I. The orbital speeds of stars in the Milky Way suggest unseen mass in a halo.
II. Dark energy was discovered because the universe's expansion is accelerating.
III. Dark energy makes up only a tiny part of the universe's energy.
Which are true?
options: I only
II only
III only
I and II only
I, II and III
quiz.why: Dark matter is the unseen halo mass shown by orbit speeds. Dark energy is the cause of accelerating expansion and makes up the majority of the energy, so III is false.
quiz.source: Slides 5-6; Top Hat sep8 page 1 (rotation curve)

quiz.q: Earth's equatorial radius is 6,378 km and Earth turns once every 24 hours. Use circumference = 2 x pi x radius. How fast does a person on the equator move because of Earth's rotation?
options: About 1,670 km/h
About 266 km/h
About 3,340 km/h
About 40,000 km/h
About 0.46 km/h
quiz.why: Circumference = 2 x pi x 6,378 km = 40,074 km. Speed = distance / time = 40,074 km / 24 h = about 1,670 km/h. Forgetting the 2 x pi gives 266 km/h, and forgetting to divide by the time gives 40,000.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 1.4 Example 1; slide 5 (more than 1,000 km/h)

quiz.q: Earth's average distance from the Sun is 1.5 x 10^8 km, and it completes one orbit in 1 year (8,760 hours). About how fast does Earth travel along its orbit?
options: About 17,000 km/h
About 1.1 x 10^5 km/h
About 2.2 x 10^5 km/h
About 9.4 x 10^8 km/h
About 3.9 x 10^7 km/h
quiz.why: The orbit's circumference is 2 x pi x 1.5 x 10^8 km = 9.4 x 10^8 km. Dividing by 8,760 h gives about 1.07 x 10^5 km/h, about 107,000 km/h. Forgetting the 2 x pi gives 17,000, and dividing by one day instead of one year gives 3.9 x 10^7.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 1.4 Example 2; slide 5 (107,000 km/h)

quiz.q: Which list orders these motions from slowest to fastest?
options: Earth's rotation, Sun's motion among nearby stars, Earth's orbit around the Sun, Solar System's orbit around the Milky Way
Sun's motion among nearby stars, Earth's rotation, Solar System's orbit around the Milky Way, Earth's orbit around the Sun
Earth's rotation, Earth's orbit around the Sun, Sun's motion among nearby stars, Solar System's orbit around the Milky Way
Solar System's orbit around the Milky Way, Earth's orbit around the Sun, Sun's motion among nearby stars, Earth's rotation
Earth's orbit around the Sun, Earth's rotation, Solar System's orbit around the Milky Way, Sun's motion among nearby stars
quiz.why: About 1,000 km/h, then 70,000, then 107,000, then 800,000 km/h. Each is bigger than the one before.
quiz.source: Slide 5; Top Hat sep8 page 1 (question 2)

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a motion we observe in the universe?
options: The Solar System orbits the Milky Way galaxy.
The Milky Way galaxy orbits the center of the Local Group.
Galaxies generally move away from each other, especially at larger distances.
The Sun orbits around the center of its local stellar neighbourhood.
The Earth spins daily and orbits the Sun once per year.
quiz.why: Nearby stars drift in essentially random directions relative to each other. They do not orbit a centre of the neighbourhood. The Milky Way and Andromeda do move around within the Local Group.
quiz.source: Slide 5; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q6 (practice, options reordered)

quiz.q: Why don't the patterns of stars in the night sky seem to change from night to night?
options: The stars are fixed on the celestial sphere and do not move in space.
The stars move together from west to east, so we do not notice.
The stars do move, but they are so far away that the motion is not noticeable over a night.
Existing stars never change position because nearby objects do not pull on them.
All the stars we see are in the same part of the Milky Way as the Sun, so they move together.
quiz.why: Stars do move (about 70,000 km/h relative to us in the local neighbourhood), but they are so far away that constellations take 10,000+ years to change noticeably.
quiz.source: Slide 5 (10,000+ years); ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q8 (practice)

quiz.q: Which statement about how we see stars in the night sky is TRUE?
options: Polaris can be seen at night from any latitude.
At the North or South Pole there are no circumpolar stars.
The constellations you see depend on both your latitude and your longitude.
Only about half of the stars in the night sky are visible on a given night, because Earth blocks the other half.
Stars rise in the west and set in the east.
quiz.why: The ground blocks half the celestial sphere, so we see only half the sky at any time. The sky depends on latitude only, and at the poles every visible star is circumpolar.
quiz.source: Slides 9-10; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q9 (practice, options rewritten)

quiz.q: The picture shows how altitude is measured in your local sky. You see a star at an altitude of 80 degrees. How many arcminutes is it from your zenith?
quiz.why: Zenith is at 90 degrees, so the star is 90 - 80 = 10 degrees from it. 10 degrees x 60 arcminutes per degree = 600 arcminutes.
quiz.source: Slide 9; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q11 (practice)

img.alt: A dome-shaped sky over a person with the horizon at 0 degrees, the zenith at 90 degrees and a star at 60 degrees altitude.

quiz.q: The two headlights of a car are 1.5 m apart. Use angular size = physical size x 360 degrees / (2 x pi x distance). About what is their angular separation, in arcminutes, when the car is 500 m away?
options: About 0.17 arcminutes
About 21 arcminutes
About 65 arcminutes
About 10 arcminutes
About 620 arcminutes
quiz.why: 1.5 x 360 / (2 x pi x 500) = 540 / 3,142 = 0.17 degrees. Multiply by 60 arcminutes per degree: about 10 arcminutes, a third of the Moon's width. The answer 0.17 forgets to convert units, and 65 forgets the 2 x pi.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 2.1 Example 1; slide 9

img.alt: An eye looking at an object that looks smaller as it moves away, and a circle showing a small object as a small piece of the circle.

quiz.q: The Moon spans about 0.5 degrees in our sky and is about 380,000 km away. Use the small-angle formula to estimate the Moon's diameter.
options: About 330 km
About 1,700 km
About 6,600 km
About 3,300 km
About 1,200,000 km
quiz.why: Diameter = angular size x 2 x pi x distance / 360 = 0.5 x 2 x pi x 380,000 / 360 = about 3,300 km (the true value is 3,476 km). Leaving out the division by 360 gives about 1,200,000 km, and using pi instead of 2 x pi gives about 1,700 km.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 2.1 Example 2; slide 9

quiz.q: Which statement about the ecliptic is FALSE?
options: The zodiac constellations lie along the ecliptic, along with one other constellation.
It represents the Sun's daily path through the sky.
It is an old concept from ancient Babylonian astronomy.
It is tilted 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator.
It is not a real path in space, but the Sun's apparent motion in our sky.
quiz.why: The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent path around the celestial sphere over a year, not its daily path. It is tilted 23.5 degrees because Earth's axis is.
quiz.source: Slide 8; Textbook 2.1; ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q12 (practice; options A and C are not on the slides)

quiz.q: What is the galactic plane?
options: A fast spacecraft built for interstellar travel.
The narrow section of the Milky Way that is visible from our vantage point on Earth.
The plane of the Local Group that contains both our galaxy and Andromeda.
The plane containing the Sun and Earth, tilted 60 degrees to the Milky Way.
The plane of the Milky Way galaxy, tilted about 63 degrees to the celestial equator.
quiz.why: The galactic plane is the flat plane of our galaxy's disk. We see it edge-on from inside as the Milky Way band, which circles the whole celestial sphere. It is tilted to the celestial equator, by about 63 degrees.
quiz.source: ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q13 (practice; the 63 degrees is not in the slides or textbook text, outside source); slides 8-9; textbook 2.1 and Figure 2.5

quiz.q: The picture shows the sky at two latitudes. You see the north celestial pole 35 degrees above your northern horizon. At its highest point, where is the celestial equator in your sky?
options: 55 degrees above the southern horizon
35 degrees above the southern horizon
55 degrees above the northern horizon
35 degrees above the northern horizon
At your zenith (90 degrees)
quiz.why: The altitude of the visible pole equals your latitude, so you are at 35 degrees N. The zenith is 90 degrees up, and the celestial equator crosses the southern sky 35 degrees away from it, so its highest point is 90 - 35 = 55 degrees above the southern horizon. At the equator (latitude 0) it would pass through the zenith.
quiz.source: Slide 10 and textbook 2.1 Figures 2.12-2.13 (pole altitude equals latitude); the equator step is derived geometry (outside source)

img.alt: Two globes: at the North Pole the north celestial pole is overhead, and at 34 degrees south latitude the south celestial pole is 34 degrees above the horizon.

quiz.q: At latitude 40 degrees N the north celestial pole is 40 degrees above your northern horizon. A star lies 25 degrees from the pole and circles it every day. Which statement is true?
options: It rises in the east and sets in the west.
It never rises above the horizon.
It never sets, and its lowest point is 15 degrees above the horizon.
It never sets, and its lowest point is 25 degrees above the horizon.
It never sets, and its lowest point is 65 degrees above the horizon.
quiz.why: The star circles the pole at 25 degrees from it, so its altitude ranges from 40 - 25 = 15 degrees (lowest) to 40 + 25 = 65 degrees (highest). Since 15 degrees is above the horizon, it never sets and is circumpolar. The 65 degrees is its highest point, not its lowest.
quiz.source: Slide 10 and textbook 2.1 Figure 2.10 (circumpolar stars, pole altitude equals latitude); lowest-altitude step is derived (outside source)

img.alt: The local sky at latitude 40 degrees north with a horizon plane cutting the celestial sphere, one circumpolar circle fully above it and one star never seen.

quiz.q: What happens to the constellations in your night sky over six months?
options: The times they rise and set change, but the same constellations remain visible.
Some constellations change, because the Sun is then at the opposite end of the ecliptic.
Northern constellations are replaced by southern ones.
Constellations that were circumpolar stop being circumpolar.
There are no major changes.
quiz.why: Earth's orbit moves the Sun along the ecliptic. After six months it is on the opposite side, so we look at night in a different direction in space and see different constellations.
quiz.source: Textbook 2.1 (variation with time of year); ASTR 207 In-Class Test 1 Q10 (practice); not covered on the slides (outside source for slides; textbook 2.1 and practice test)

order.prompt: Put these levels of our cosmic address in order from the smallest (bottom) to the largest (top).
order.why: Earth is about 10,000 km across. The Solar System is about 10^10 km (about 60 AU) across, and the Milky Way about 100,000 light-years. The Local Group is about 3 million light-years across and the Local Supercluster about 100 million light-years. The universe contains all of them.

order.prompt: Put these motions in order from the slowest (bottom) to the fastest (top).
order.why: Earth's spin at the equator is about 1,670 km/h. The Sun drifts among nearby stars at about 70,000 km/h, Earth orbits the Sun at about 107,000 km/h, the Milky Way approaches Andromeda at about 300,000 km/h, and the Solar System orbits the Milky Way at about 800,000 km/h.

order.title: The cosmic calendar, earliest to latest
order.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen on the one-year cosmic calendar, earliest at the bottom and latest at the top.
order.why: The Big Bang is on Jan 1 and the Milky Way forms in February. Earth forms on Sept 3, the Cambrian explosion is on Dec 17 and the dinosaurs die out on Dec 30. Modern humans only appear at 11:58 PM on Dec 31.

sort.prompt: Is each distance better measured in astronomical units (AU) or in light-years (ly)?

items.text: Distance from Earth to the Sun
Distance from the Sun to Jupiter
Distance from the Sun to Neptune
The size of Earth's orbit
How far the planets are spread out around the Sun
Distance from the Sun to Alpha Centauri
Distance across the Milky Way
Distance to the Andromeda Galaxy
Distance to the Orion Nebula
Distance to the most distant galaxies seen by JWST

sort.why: The astronomical unit (150 million km) is handy inside the Solar System. The light-year (about 10 trillion km) is used for stars and galaxies, where distances in AU would be huge numbers.

sort.title: Real motion or only an appearance?
sort.prompt: Is each item a real motion in space or only an appearance (an illusion from our view of the sky)?

items.text: Earth spinning west to east
Earth orbiting the Sun
The Solar System orbiting the center of the Milky Way
The Milky Way and Andromeda approaching each other
Distant galaxies moving away from us
Stars rising in the east and setting in the west
The celestial sphere turning around Earth
The Sun moving along the ecliptic through the year
All the stars in a constellation lying at the same distance
The Sun and Moon looking the same size in the sky
Stars fixed on a giant sphere

sort.why: Earth really spins and orbits, the Solar System really circles the galaxy, and galaxies really move. Stars rising and setting, the turning celestial sphere and the Sun's path along the ecliptic come from Earth's own motion. The sphere, equal star distances and equal Sun and Moon sizes are effects of having no depth perception in space.
